verdicts.trueWording: the area is not an encounter and should not be assigned
verdicts.note: Live PDF (HTTP 200, 6pp, pdftotext -layout). Appendix II, 'The Adventure's Encounters (Mandatory)': if you have nothing to say for any of the listed categories (Read-aloud Text, General Description, Creature(s), Tactics, Trap(s), Treasure, Development, Ad-Hoc XP), the area is not an encounter and gets no encounter number. Both limbs -- nothing to say under any heading, and no number -- supported; the next sentence adds that editors dislike printing 'This room is empty.'

verdicts.trueWording: compelling fantasy city is presenting a strong "sense of place"
verdicts.note: Appendix 1: Cities of Adventure, opening line under the heading THIRTY QUESTIONS ABOUT YOUR CITY. Quote matches word for word including the curly quotation marks around the phrase; attribution to the DUNGEON staff is the document's own voice.

Appendix 1 heading verbatim. Every limb supported: the lead-in directs the writer to answer the 30 questions before starting the Cities of Adventure submission, and the list opens with question 1 on who rules the city and question 2 on how the ruler maintains power. Counted the list -- it runs 1 to 30.

verdicts.trueWording: What does the city smell like?
verdicts.note: Appendix 1, question 24, verbatim and at the claimed number. Framing limb is directive rather than a stated mandate: the lead-in is an imperative ('develop a familiarity with your locale by answering the following 30 questions') and the Features entry says 'take some time to answer the questions in Appendix 1' -- not labelled Mandatory the way adventure sections are. 'Require' is a fair gloss on the imperative, so no limb is unsupported.

verdicts.trueWording: WHY DO ADVENTURERS COME TO YOUR CITY?
verdicts.note: Appendix 1, question 30, verbatim. Both distinguishing limbs checked mechanically against the extracted text: it is the last of the thirty, and a regex scan of questions 1-30 found question 30 the only one set in capitals (the all-caps section heading is not a question).

verdicts.trueWording: Cities of Adventure articles range in length from 8,000-10,000 words
verdicts.note: Features section, Cities of Adventure entry. Quote verbatim; the sentence completes with the 8,000-10,000 word range the claim states (en dash in the original, not 'to').

verdicts.trueWording: brief appendix with up to five complete stat blocks
verdicts.note: Features, Cities of Adventure: the finished article 'should include' a brief appendix with up to five complete stat blocks for personages important to the city. Quote verbatim; the claim's 'must' is a slight hardening of the guidelines' 'should include', but the requirement and every other limb (brief appendix, up to five, complete, personages important to the city) is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: present an adventure background in 500 words, it's probably too complex
verdicts.note: Appendix II, Adventure Background (Mandatory). Quote verbatim (curly apostrophe in original); the sentence ends 'and should be simplified', supporting that limb, and the following sentence caps the background at 5% of total length.

verdicts.trueWording: detail rumors, background information the players can uncover in research
verdicts.note: Appendix II, The Adventure's Encounters (Mandatory). Quote verbatim. The page's phrasing is 'At the start of the adventure's encounters, you can include additional sections that detail rumors, background information the players can uncover in research or by using bardic knowledge checks, town statistics...' -- all three listed items present ('rumors', US spelling), and 'at the start of' carries the claim's 'before an adventure's encounters'.

verdicts.trueWording: we will not publish an article written in the first person
verdicts.note: Live HTML fetched with a browser user agent (HTTP 200). Under the 'Format and Style' heading, verbatim, preceded by 'Note that'. The following sentences forbid 'I' or 'my' unless spoken by a character other than the author, confirming the rule's strength.

verdicts.trueWording: it should be no more than 200 words long
verdicts.note: Format and Style: 'If your article begins with a narrative vignette or piece of example dialog, it should be no more than 200 words long.' Quote verbatim; both limbs of the claim (narrative vignette, example dialogue) and the 200-word cap are on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: Article manuscripts should use the current style of D&D game products
verdicts.note: Format and Style, first paragraph. Quote verbatim, and the very next sentence supplies both remaining limbs: names of magic items and spells should be italicized, and feat names should be capitalized. Claim's 'require' renders the guidelines' 'should'.

verdicts.trueWording: As an editor, I cut weasel words without mercy.
verdicts.note: Live WordPress page (HTTP 200), post dated July 14 2020, sentence verbatim under the 'Hedging' heading. The quoted assertion is fully supported. The appositive describing Sims is not: the page identifies him only as 'an editor and technical editor (also called developer in some places)' and, in footnote 4, says he began 'working on D&D' after 2000. Wizards of the Coast appears on the page only in an art credit and an ad reference, never as his employer, so the employment limb cannot be verified from this page.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that Sims is 'a D&D editor at Wizards of the Coast' -- the page states only 'editor and technical editor' and that he 'started working on D&D'; it never names WotC as his employer

verdicts.trueWording: words such as generally, typically, and similar weasels
verdicts.note: Footnote 3 of the same post, verbatim: he has 'a thing against' such words, calling them long and slippery enough to resemble their namesake. Supports both named examples and the objection.

verdicts.trueWording: yet to see a superlative that was necessary for the fiction
verdicts.note: Under 'Superlatives or Absolutisms', verbatim: 'I've yet to see a superlative that was necessary for the fiction or mechanic in which the absolute appears.' Only divergence is the closing noun -- the page says 'in which the absolute appears' where the claim says 'in which it appeared', a pronoun for the same superlative-created absolute; no limb unsupported.
